title: Trump Brushes Off Netanyahu's Opposition to F-35 Fighter Jet Sale to Turkey
excerpt: As Netanyahu arrives in Washington for a high-stakes meeting, Trump declares 'nobody tells me what we should be selling' and calls Turkey a 'tremendous ally,' deepening a rift between the longtime partners.
body:
• Trump dismissed Netanyahu's objections to a potential F-35 sale to Turkey, saying "nobody" dictates US arms sales
  • Netanyahu has warned the sale would "destroy the power balance in the Middle East" and called Turkey's government hostile to Israeli interests
  • The dispute is one of several flashpoints straining the US-Israel relationship ahead of Netanyahu's Washington visit this week
  • Turkey was removed from the F-35 program in 2019 after purchasing Russia's S-400 missile defense system

Trump Asserts Sole Authority on Arms Sales

President Donald Trump rejected Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's public campaign against a potential sale of F-35 stealth fighter jets to Turkey, declaring on Monday that no foreign leader has a say in American arms deals.

"Nobody tells me what we should be selling," Trump told reporters when asked about Netanyahu's opposition, according to CNN. He described Turkey as a "tremendous ally," a characterization that stands in sharp contrast to Israel's view of the NATO member under President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

The exchange laid bare a growing divide between the two leaders on a deal that could reshape military dynamics across the Middle East — and it came just hours before Netanyahu departed for Washington, where the two are expected to meet on the sidelines of Senator Lindsey Graham's funeral.

Israel's Security Concerns

Netanyahu has been vocal in opposing the sale, telling CNN in a recent interview that providing advanced stealth aircraft to Turkey would "destroy the power balance in the Middle East because Turkey has aggressive aspirations." He went further, calling Erdogan's government "infected with the Muslim Brotherhood" and arguing that Turkey is neither a "friendly state" nor a "model ally" of the United States, according to TBS News.

Israeli officials have framed their opposition around the concept of Israel's "qualitative military edge" — a longstanding principle in US defense policy that ensures Israel maintains a technological advantage over its regional adversaries. The F-35, manufactured by Lockheed Martin, is considered the most advanced fighter jet in the world.

"It would destroy the power balance in the Middle East because Turkey has aggressive aspirations."

— Benjamin Netanyahu, Israeli Prime Minister

The friction over the F-35 sale has already produced concrete fallout. US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth canceled a scheduled meeting with Netanyahu earlier this month to discuss the potential deal, according to Reuters. Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz was also due to meet Hegseth during a trip to Israel.

Turkey's Path Back to the F-35 Program

Turkey was originally a partner in the multinational F-35 program and had six aircraft built and allocated for delivery. But the US suspended Ankara's participation in 2019 after Turkey purchased Russia's S-400 air defense system, which Washington said posed risks to the F-35's sensitive stealth technology.

At a NATO summit in Turkey earlier this month, Trump signaled he was considering reversing the ban and lifting US sanctions imposed on Ankara over the S-400 purchase. Erdogan, for his part, dismissed Israeli and Greek objections to the deal, telling reporters that such concerns "have no place in my world," according to The Defense News.

When asked whether Turkey would give up the Russian-made S-400 system to secure the F-35 deal, Erdogan declined to answer directly, telling reporters to "keep watching."

A Relationship Under Strain

The F-35 dispute is far from the only source of tension between Trump and Netanyahu. The two leaders' relationship has shifted markedly since the early months of the Iran conflict, when they coordinated closely on military operations. As the war dragged into a stalemate, Trump grew frustrated with the outcome, and an April ceasefire exposed deep disagreements over strategy.

Vice President JD Vance has accused members of Netanyahu's cabinet of working to sabotage the Iran negotiations, warning that Israel is "alienating the only powerful ally they have left," according to CNN. Trump himself has called Netanyahu "crazy" and "difficult" in connection with continued Israeli military operations in Lebanon.

Netanyahu, however, has dismissed the disagreements as "tactical," insisting the partnership remains strong. An Israeli source told CNN that Netanyahu will seek assurances during this visit that any arms sales to Turkey won't compromise Israel's military edge, along with progress on a new long-term US-Israel defense pact to replace the Obama-era memorandum set to expire.

What's Next

The meeting between Trump and Netanyahu — expected to take place this week in Washington — will test whether personal diplomacy can bridge a widening gap on multiple fronts. Netanyahu faces reelection in October and needs to demonstrate continued influence in Washington. Trump, aware of this leverage, has selectively shown support while maintaining pressure.

Any decision on the F-35 sale to Turkey would still face strong resistance in the US Congress, where bipartisan skepticism of Ankara's defense posture remains deep. But Trump's public dismissal of Israeli objections suggests the administration is treating the matter as a bilateral US-Turkey decision — not one that requires Jerusalem's approval.
